assumptions.summary: No natural retirement/firing; staff make leave decisions and have latent traits.
Monthly decisions flow through an assumed Human Capital network.
Allocation rules infer position levels and office heads.
Higher positions have more concentrated priors and distance reduces information by squared path length.
Promotion precedes recruitment when qualification permits.
Experience thresholds, six-month posting, nine percent effort and deterministic costs support simulation.
25/35 percent churn scenarios adjust prior ratios and seek 80 percent fill.
No-recruitment health uses uniform experience and one-quarter qualified per level.
Shared cognition is separable/additive in co-working pairs.

language_observations.summary: The reusable human writing moves are task decomposition, explicit premises before formulas, a small intuitive example before transfer, honest parameter exposure, curve-to-mechanism interpretation, matched comparison and a named data boundary.

the Summary turns churn pressure into a state-to-policy route: Name the human-capital graph, probabilistic churn, promotion choices, recruitment controls, productivity/cost outputs, then close with health, layers and volatility.
a broad management question is decomposed into visible analytical jobs: Enumerate network construction, churn/HR mechanisms, sustainability, health, team layers and sensitivity before solving them.

latent individual behaviour is made modelable through explicit assumptions: State no forced exits, hidden characteristics, networked decision information and HR authority before defining a monthly state.

an incomplete organization diagram becomes a position graph through declared allocation rules: Show the level-allocation assumptions, table, node set and edge conditions, then visualize the resulting information network.
notation fixes the people-position-time handoff before probability is introduced: Define leaving, recruitment, workforce mapping and graph distance so later monthly updates have a stable domain.

a simple conjugate-learning example prepares the reader for a churn mechanism: Walk from Bernoulli draw to Beta prior and update, explain why the posterior learns, then transfer only the needed structure to leaving decisions.

an annual churn target becomes level-specific uncertainty through a prior: Convert annual rate to monthly leave chance, use alpha plus beta to control variance, and explain why senior positions are modeled as less volatile.

network distance is used to weaken social information before it changes a decision: State that nearby resignations matter more, decay the update by squared path distance, and carry the result into the next-period parameters.

a stochastic employee decision is followed by an explicit manager branch: Sample stay/leave, pool neighbours' outcomes, update the prior, then hand vacancies to a manager who must prefer promotion before recruitment.

three promotion criteria convert imperfect information into a comparable management choice: Start with experience under ignorance, then replace the ranking key with leave likelihood or centrality while keeping qualification and vacancy conditions fixed.

simulation inputs are exposed as a compact ledger before curves are interpreted: List experience thresholds, post renewal interval, priors, recruiting effort and deterministic cost premise before presenting any output.

organizational productivity is built from level, experience and dissatisfaction before loss is decomposed: Define individual contribution, normalize memory-weighted dissatisfaction, weight positions by centrality, then separate direct departure loss from indirect morale loss.

plots are read with a causal story and a cost boundary: Use distributions to show level churn and five-year drift, connect direct/indirect loss to resignations, then keep salary outside the displayed recruitment/training budget.

same-axis churn scenarios reveal both capacity loss and the recruiting control needed to counter it: Compare 18, 25 and 35 percent paths, read staff/productivity/cost together, then adjust posting interval and effort to restore an 80 percent staffing target.

an extreme no-recruitment case is narrowed to a health visualization: Acknowledge obvious aggregate decline, focus on office-level fill percentages, show the time snapshots, and explain why low tiers fail without external entry.

a comparative table separates staff retention from productivity before recommending a promotion policy: Hold the baseline experience rule visible, read centrality and likelihood changes by year, and state the modest retention versus larger productivity differences.

team science and multilayers are presented as conditional extensions rather than completed evidence: Define shared cognition and training as possible productivity mechanisms, distinguish position and people layers, then stop where data prevent simulation.

a local parameter sweep is followed by an explanation of what remains unknown: Sweep alpha, distinguish insensitive productivity from sensitive indirect/direct ratio, connect alpha to psychological mechanisms, then request empirical research.

the conclusion compresses strengths and named limits without adding new proof: Pair simple flexible simulation with volatility, unrealistic productivity premises and missing team cognition, then restate only the validated workflow.

results_trace.summary: Middle-manager churn is roughly 30 percent, other levels about 15 percent and overall median moves from 18 to 20 percent over five years.
A resignation is reported as about 20 units direct and 25 units indirect loss against monthly 2000-2500 productivity units.
Recruitment and training costs average about 7 and 37 sigma every six months while salary is omitted from the displayed budget.
At 25 and 35 percent churn, long-run staff settle around 60 and 40 percent fill; revised intervals/effort seek 80 percent fill.
No recruitment leaves around 204 people after two years and lower tiers lose health first.
Likelihood gives 2.61 percent more staff than experience by Year 10; centrality and likelihood increase reported productivity by over 11 percent.
A 50 percent alpha change shifts calculated productivity by no more than five percent in most runs but changes indirect/direct ratio materially.
The source explicitly names volatility, unrealistic assumptions and omitted team cognition.
Conclusion restates conditional organizational heuristics rather than independent evidence.

source.title: Organizational Churn: A Roll of the Dice?

source_quality.summary: All 21 physical pages were read twice and visually reviewed. The paper moves from a reconstructed 370-position graph through Bayesian churn, manager reactions, productivity/cost scenarios, health visualization, comparative promotions, conditional team/multilayer extensions and named volatility limits.

decisions: how to represent churn, how to rank promotions/recruitment, how to read capacity/health and what evidence is needed before deployment
inputs: 370-position hierarchy, churn situation, organization diagram, recruitment/training information and management scenarios
outputs: position graph, monthly churn and HR event process, productivity/cost proxies, capacity/health/promotion comparisons and conditional network extensions

title: Organizational Churn: A Roll of the Dice?
unresolved_questions: The Summary calls the model powerful and reliable, but all productivity, cost and HR-health claims remain paper-internal simulations.
The task decomposition assumes hidden staff traits, a Human Capital network and HR authority without a released personnel or governance record.
The 370-position allocation table follows reasonable assumptions, but the source does not validate the inferred levels, office heads or graph edges.
The Bernoulli/Beta teaching example is mathematically familiar but does not establish that individual churn follows the chosen prior or independent draws.
Level-specific alpha and beta, annual-to-month conversion and inverse-square information reduction are assumed; distances, disconnected cases and social exposure are not calibrated.
The churn algorithm omits random seed, simultaneous-event policy, update ordering and protections against using inferred leave risk unfairly.
Experience, likelihood and centrality promotion strategies lack capability validation, tie rules, fairness metrics, privacy safeguards and subgroup outcomes.
The upward churn adjustment is a tractable modification, not evidence that the organization has the stated five-year trend.
Dissatisfaction combines memory decay and graph distance with an unsupported citation placeholder; its alpha value is not independently identified.
Salary, training and closeness-weighted productivity plus direct/indirect loss are constructed proxies with no units, observed outcomes or uncertainty propagation.
Fifty simulated churn runs and displayed six-month costs omit seeds, raw series, salary totals and confidence intervals.
The 18/25/35 percent scenarios and recruitment adjustments target 80 percent fill, but the tolerance, costs, capacity constraints and external validation are missing.
No-external-recruitment health colors and the 204.01 arithmetic check depend on uniform experience and assumed promotion eligibility.
Table 2 reports promotion differences through Year 10 but does not show replication, uncertainty, productivity units or effects on workers denied promotion.
Shared cognition and team training are proposed informally; pair weights, empirical measures and causal productivity effects are not supplied.
Friendship, trust, supervision and teammate layers are described without observed edge data; the paper correctly stops short of simulation.
Alpha sensitivity reports productivity as locally insensitive and indirect/direct ratio as sensitive, but no decision tolerance or empirical alpha estimate is given.
Claimed simplicity, flexibility and appealing simulations do not overcome volatility, linear-training and role-preference assumptions, or omitted team cognition.
The conclusion restates workflow and comparative gains but supplies no independent validation beyond the model's own assumptions and traces.
